prime.problem: "Supports JSON Schema" can mean an engine rejects most real schemas, accepts them and then times out, or accepts them and quietly ignores a keyword. One number can't tell those apart, so picking an engine by a single headline score picks the wrong failure.
prime.fits: First card of part 5. The schema card listed which keywords are hard; the compile and mask cards showed why some engines stall. This card measures the outcome across thousands of real schemas, and the next card splits the failures into too strict and too loose.
expect: the conservative strategy of hosted APIs
why true coverage can't be measured
prime.goal: Read an engine's coverage and compliance together, say which kind of failure each engine has, and design a test on your own schemas.

attend: Why is empirical coverage always at most declared coverage, and what sits in the gap?
OpenAI scores 1.00 compliance on GitHub-Hard. Why is that both reassuring and a problem?
Where did most of Outlines' "accepted then failed" schemas go, and which schema features caused it?
Why is LM-only's compliance simply equal to its empirical coverage?
Why can a single invalid output disprove true coverage, while 30 valid outputs can't prove it?

must: Declared = schemas accepted without error → empirical = schemas whose output validated → compliance = empirical ÷ declared → coverage says how much an engine will try, compliance says whether "accepted" can be trusted

Hosted APIs support only features they can reliably enforce → they reject most hard schemas up front (OpenAI declares 0.09 on GitHub-Hard) → what they accept almost always complies (1.00) → you get an error, not silent bad output, but often an error
An engine that accepts everything, then compiles or generates too slowly → timeouts count as failures (Outlines: 47 accepted, 3 valid on GitHub-Hard) → high declared coverage with very low compliance

True coverage means the constraint equals the schema for every possible output → infinitely many outputs → it can only be disproved (Ollama ignoring multipleOf) → test your own schemas and keep validating
elevated: The numbers are top-1 greedy outputs on a 1B model with 40 s timeouts, from late-2024 engine versions → sampling more outputs "might detect more schema violations" → treat them as ranking evidence, not as your pass rate
reference: the two Outlines compliance cells that don't recompute (GitHub-Easy, Snowplow)

compress.prompt: From memory, draw one bar per engine for GitHub-Hard split into three parts: rejected up front, accepted then failed, accepted and valid. Then write the compliance formula and one sentence on what each extreme (OpenAI, Outlines) is bad at.
checklist: declared = accepted; empirical = accepted and valid; compliance = their ratio
OpenAI: 91 of 100 rejected, 9 accepted, all 9 valid
Outlines: 53 rejected, 47 accepted, only 3 valid (mostly timeouts)
true coverage can't be measured, only disproved

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between coverage and compliance in one sentence each, then say why you need both.
answer: coverage: the share of schemas the engine takes (declared) or gets right (empirical)
compliance: of the schemas it takes, the share that come out valid
high compliance on few schemas and high coverage with low compliance are opposite failures; one number hides which one you have

retrieve.q: Turn GitHub-Hard's rows into counts per 100 schemas for Guidance, OpenAI and Outlines: rejected, accepted-then-failed, valid.
answer: Guidance: 40 rejected, 19 accepted then failed, 41 valid (0.41 / 0.60 ≈ 0.68)

retrieve.q: Your team must pick between a hosted strict mode (low coverage, compliance 1.00) and a self-hosted engine (higher coverage, compliance 0.7–0.9). What decides it, and what do you add around each?
answer: whether your schemas fall inside the API's subset: if they do, you get near-perfect compliance
if they don't, the API rejects them and you need prompt + repair, or a self-hosted engine
around the self-hosted engine: a validator on every output, because compliance under 1.00 means some accepted schemas still fail

compare.q: Coverage counts schemas; the over/under card counts keyword categories in a test suite. Why do the two rankings disagree, and which should drive your choice?
answer: real schemas use a few keywords a lot and most rarely
a test suite weighs every keyword category equally
the paper: "no straightforward correspondence" between the two
drive the choice with your own schemas; use the test suite to learn which keywords to double-check

compare.q: LM-only has declared coverage 1.00 everywhere. Why is that meaningless, and what does its empirical coverage (0.90 → 0.13) tell you instead?
answer: it enforces nothing, so it "accepts" every schema by default
its compliance equals its empirical coverage
empirical coverage shows how often a free-running model happens to match: fine on easy schemas, poor on hard ones

predict.q: The paper's open engines ran greedy, one output per schema. If it had sampled 10 outputs per schema at temperature 0.7 and counted a schema as covered only if all 10 validated, which number would move most, and for which kind of engine? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Empirical coverage (and so compliance) would fall, and it would fall most for loose engines. An engine whose constraint truly matches a schema produces valid output at any temperature. An under-constrained engine relies on the model to stay valid where the grammar doesn't enforce it, and more samples give it more chances to slip. The paper itself says sampling more outputs "might detect more schema violations". Declared coverage wouldn't change at all, since it's decided before generation.

apply.task: Design a coverage test for your own stack. Pick 5 schemas you really use (or the order schema plus 4 variants that add multipleOf, maximum, format: email and a recursive $ref). For each, record: accepted or rejected, and for accepted ones, 3 sampled outputs validated with jsonschema (format checks on). Compute your declared coverage, empirical coverage and compliance.
apply.done: You have a 5-row table and three numbers, and for each failure you can say whether it was a rejection, an invalid output, or a keyword the engine accepted but ignored.
apply.hint: If you use Ollama, the course's checks predict: all 5 accepted, multipleOf, maximum and format not enforced (so those can come out invalid), and the recursive schema accepted. Only count an output invalid if jsonschema rejects it.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: which number moves when you sample more outputs?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why 1.00 compliance can be a bad sign?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: accepted → enforced, or enforced → valid?
Which of your own schemas would a conservative hosted API reject today?
What will you look for in the over/under card: which keywords make an engine too loose, and which too strict?
